Dyspareunia without discharge, itching, or visible lesions further supports a *neuropathic* rather than infectious-inflammatory cause — consistent with possible sacral radicular involvement (e.g., S2–S4). The temporal clustering, strict dermatomal distribution, and absence of mucocutaneous lesions in two of three regions strongly point to **disseminated varicella-zoster virus (VZV) reactivation**, specifically **zoster sine herpete** — a well-documented entity where VZV causes radicular pain and neurologic dysfunction without vesicular rash in one or more involved dermatomes. The presence of *intact* forearm blisters (C6–C7) provides direct virologic access for PCR confirmation — the gold standard for active VZV infection. MRI of the trigeminal nerve is indicated to detect subclinical nerve enhancement (a known finding in zoster-related trigeminal neuropathy), and pending VZV PCR, empiric antivirals are justified per guidelines for high-suspicion zoster sine herpete.
